::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: To assess psychological tests and scales for violations of intergroup comparability -termed Measurement Non-Invariance (MNI) in factor analysis and Differential Item Functioning (DIF) in item response theory -statistical testing has emerged as the dominant approach, but inherently fails to differentiate between major and negligible violations.

In response to this, upwards of 37 effect size measures for both MNI and DIF have been proposed over the last decades, using vastly different conventions in naming and notation, with no clear consensus on interpretation.
This arguably constitutes a severe hindrance for the much-needed popularization of non-dichotomous assessments of intergroup comparability.
We address this by systematically deriving a unified framework for a large class of measures from the theoretical definition of first-order measurement invariance.
This yields a rich and interpretable taxonomic framework derived from just four fundamental types:

Expected Difference (ED), Expected Absolute Difference (EAD), Total Expected Difference (TED) and Total Expected Absolute Difference (TEAD), which are universally applicable, irrespective of the underlying measurement model.
Seen as instances of these four measures, this framework includes the 37 identified measures, uncovering both a notable 'Jangle' and vast taxonomic gaps in the literature.

Finally, we show the relations between measures of this framework and provide a step-by-step guide for practical applications, which we illustrate using models of both factor analysis and item response theory on real-world data.
Psychological research commonly revolves around the quantitative measurement of unobservable constructs such as personality traits or psychopathologies.

Conceptualized as continuous latent variables, they are measured indirectly through indicators -observable variables assumed to be correlated with the latent traits of interest -usually items on questionnaires and tests.
A major caveat of the latent variable paradigm is that valid intergroup comparability is not guaranteed by default.

For instance, there is evidence that after-treatment scores on depression scales overestimate depressive symptomatology, introducing longitudinal bias that may confound evaluation of treatment efficacy (Fokkema et al., 2013).

text.text: In cross-cultural research, acquiescence has been shown to be considerably higher in countries with stronger social norms of deference (Lechner et al., 2019).

text.text: Age and gender differences (Sharp et al., 2014) are also typical sources of such biases.

text.text: A priori, group-specific differences in response behavior may be present in any relevant grouping.

Without establishing that indicators measure invariantly across groups and time, observed group and longitudinal differences cannot be reliably traced back to 'true' latent differences, prompting the need to detect violations of intergroup comparability methodically.
For quantitative evaluations of intergroup comparability, the key insight is the observation that such violations manifest in distinct unobservable-observable relationships in the respective groups.
Hence, the statistical foundation is formed by group-specific latent measurement models, which separately estimate this relationship for each relevant group.

As such, investigations of intergroup comparability can be operationalized as determining differences of group-specific measurement models across groups; a lack of meaningful differences is then seen as evidence of intergroup comparability.

The most prominent latent measurement models in psychological research are derived from Factor Analysis (FA) & Item Response Theory (IRT), respectively postulating a linear & logistic or probit link between unobservable and observable variables.

text.text: Within each of these measurement paradigms, different terms are used for this statistical concept of intergroup comparability.
The presence of violations thereof is declared Measurement Non-Invariance (MNI) in FA and Differential Item/Test Functioning (DIF/DTF) in IRT.

These notions can be viewed as twin concepts (Thissen, 2025), derived from a shared latent-trait-theoretic definition (Meredith, 1993) unspecific to any measurement model type, although it should be noted that the frameworks of MNI and DIF/DTF are not fully interchangeable; Measurement Invariance (MI), the lack of MNI, is typically tested for in stages -starting from configural MI, then weak MI, followed by strong MI and finally strict MI -an approach with no equivalent in IRT.

text.text: By contrast, item-level DIF testing is a routine practice, whereas MI analyses rarely focus on differences at the item level.

In essence, group-specific model comparisons commonly operate on the parameter level, with parameters having fundamentally different interpretations in IRT and FA models, hence this differentiating terminology is justified to some degree.
Nonetheless, the core idea of comparing a more constrained (MI) model to a less constrained (MNI) model is indeed shared across model paradigms.
Dating back to as early as Dorans and Kulick (1983), there has been an ongoing trend to develop effect size measures for amounts of MNI or DIF/DTF.

text.text: Such effect-based assessments of intergroup comparability aim to capture the severity and practical impact of differences in measurement across groups, rather than relying solely on null-hypothesis significance testing, which -by design -can only ever provide evidence for the mere presence of differences.
Reviewing the literature reveals a surprisingly high number of proposed effect size measures, both for MNI and for DIF/DTF, that have accumulated over the last decades.
Throughout publications, some common themes can be identified.
First, proposals are rarely -if ever -based on theoretical definitions that specify the actual quantity being measured.
Second, specific 'design choices' in the construction of measures are rarely motivated.
Third, there seems to be no consensus on notation, nor on interpretation, despite many similarities across proposals.
Navigating this vast array of different measures is challenging, even for experts.
In this paper, we aim to systematically resolve these issues for a broad range of measures.

Based on precise mathematical definitions, we conceptually distill a large, model-agnostic class of measures theoretically derived from the concept of first-order measurement invariance (Bauer, 2017).

We show that this framework encompasses at least 37 of the measures that have been proposed throughout the last decades, revealing a notable case of the 'Jangle Fallacy' (Kelley, 1927), as well as vast taxonomic gaps in the literature.

For investigations of both MNI and DIF, by far the most common approach is using statistical tests to decide whether group-specific models fit significantly better than a single, shared one.
Here, the convention is for the null hypothesis to represent intergroup comparability, i.e., the desired presence of MI.
On a conceptual level, this has the effect of understanding intergroup comparability as a binary quality factor that, for any given indicator, must either be established or discarded.
Direct intergroup comparisons are thus either deemed justified or baseless, with a complete inability to distinguish between mild and severe violations of invariance.

This predominantly used all-or-nothing approach is particularly problematic given that higher sample size alone will increase statistical power and therefore the likelihood of non-invariance verdicts, even for potentially minuscule violations thereof.

text.text: It is indeed not always clear how to proceed when a negative result (MNI or DIF) is obtained.
This may incentivize researchers to only report results supporting comparability, meanwhile ignoring evidence for the contrary.
In summary, as a standalone tool for the investigation of intergroup comparability, it can be argued that statistical testing is insufficient in many regards.

These problems can be resolved by a fundamental reconceptualization: Instead of framing MNI and DIF as a yes-or-no question, we can instead determine its magnitude, allowing practical relevance to be quantitatively integrated in the discussion.

Recall the well-established fact that statistically significant mean differences can correspond to a practically meaningless effect in actuality -which only becomes apparent through the use of effect size measures such as Cohen's d.

text.text: All in all, there seems to be no consensus on notation, nor on interpretation.
In our view, this arguably chaotic state of research constitutes a significant hurdle for researchers intending to apply these concepts.
This, in turn, may even actively hinder the much-needed popularization of non-binary approaches to evaluating intergroup comparability.
Thus, our aim is to resolve the described issues by organizing the core concepts in a systematic and comprehensible way.
In this paper, we aim to reunite IRT and FA in effect-based assessments of intergroup comparability by introducing a novel notational framework from the ground up, which is... ...
Model-Agnostic.
All measures introduced within the framework are designed to be applicable to any latent measurement model that allows for model-implied expected responses to be calculated.
This includes the entirety of FA and IRT models.
This work is organized into eight parts.
First, we review the theoretical concept of '1 st -order MI', on which the entire taxonomic framework is based.
Second, we define the concept of an 'expected response function' which we subsequently illustrate for commonly used latent measurement models.

Third, based on the general, model-unspecific notion of expected response functions, we formally construct the framework by introducing ED & EAD for a given group's amount of 1 st -order MNI and TED & TEAD for the total, i.e., across-group amount of 1 st -order MNI when accounting for a given grouping.

text.text: Fourth, we use the framework to derive formulas for amounts of 'MNI-induced bias' in commonly used (standardized) mean difference effects.
Fifth, we summarize the core measures of our framework and show how they relate to one another.
In particular, we derive and illustrate when and why measures agree or disagree.
Sixth, we provide a step-by-step guide for the practical application and interpretation of any such effect size measures of MNI.
Seventh, we illustrate the use on one empirical example twice, using both an FA and an IRT measurement model.
Finally, in Appendix A, we provide a detailed taxonomic classification for all 37 identified measures of 1 st -order MNI in terms of our proposed framework.
In the following, we will present the latent-trait-theoretic concept underlying both the FA notion of MNI and the IRT notion of DIF/DTF.
For the rest of this paper, we will use the terminology defined as follows, making no distinction between different types of measurement models.
Latent trait theory postulates the existence of unobservable latent traits, conceptualized as variables that can be measured indirectly by relating them to responses on observable indicators.
Indirect measurement is justified by the assumption of latent trait levels inducing characteristic response behavior.
Intergroup comparability violations are commonly defined as follows.
Definition.

An indicator exhibits Measurement Non-Invariance (MNI) if it functions differently (in the sense of fixed latent trait levels inducing systematically distinct response behavior) across groups or time.

In general, the term group is used generically for any categorical partitions (e.g., according to gender or nationality) and temporal partitions (e.g., separating pre-and post-treatment) of the population.

This framework generalizes the idea of comparing group-specific response behavior to a baseline response behavior.

This idea is operationalized by comparing the expected response function R g derived from a 'non-invariant' (i.e., group-specific) measurement model, to a baseline expected response function R derived from an 'invariant' (i.e., global/reference) measurement model.
Given adequate model fit of the non-invariant model, the average difference R g ´R can be interpreted as a measure of the amount of 1 st -order non-invariance (2) relative to the 'invariant' model.
Our framework captures precisely such average expected response differences, yielding a unified class of effect size measures for the average amount of 1 st -order non-invariance.
As we have shown, this class can be described entirely by a few basal measures of group and across-group amounts of MNI.
• ED is the group average (signed) difference of expected responses.
It is especially useful to estimate how non-invariance will impact observed means, relative to the 'invariant' baseline.
• EAD is the group average absolute difference, describing the average error when using the 'invariant' model to describe the response behavior of the group.
Using squared errors instead yields the numerically simpler approximation RESD.
• TED & TEAD are the across-group average signed & absolute difference, respectively, capturing the corresponding total effect of MNI accounting for proportional group sizes.

In practice, applying the measures presented in this paper in real-world analyses of measurement non-invariance involves several steps.
To make applications more accessible, we outline this workflow in the following step-by-step guide, highlighting what needs to be considered at each stage of the analysis.
First, choose the groups in which possible non-invariances should be accounted for.

Such a partition into groups is typically determined by distinct values on one or more covariates, e.g., g " 'Germans' as one group determined by the covariate country or g " 'German Women' as one group determined by the covariates country and gender.
Different measurement occasions can also be used to determine a partition into distinct groups for which non-invariance should be accounted for.
The sample size n g of each group should be deemed sufficiently large for meaningful measurement model estimation.
The effects of non-invariance described in this paper are always relative to a baseline response behavior, thus determining a suitable baseline is crucial for the interpretability of such effects.
This may be guided by the underlying null hypothesis.
For instance, a reference group r may be an appropriate baseline in more confirmatory settings.
An example of this is comparing translations of a scale to its original.
In this case, response behavior on the original scale can be chosen as a meaningful baseline.
In more exploratory settings, when no group constitutes a meaningful default, the globally fitted response behavior usually constitutes a less artificial baseline.
Note that since such global baselines effectively pool all distinct response behaviors into a single compromise, the largest group will usually appear the most invariant.
As with any analyses of MNI, the scales of the latent factors need to be identified to ensure comparability of all relevant models (Putnick & Bornstein, 2016).

text.text: In practice, this can be realized by defining an anchor item.

Since -by definition -such an item will appear perfectly invariant across all groups, special care should be taken in choosing a suitable anchor item, for instance using cluster-based anchor item identification and selection (Pohl et al., 2021).

text.text: Given the choices of Steps 1-3, a corresponding 'non-invariant' (i.e., less restricted) multi-group model needs to be estimated for the group-specific response behavior.
The fit of this model should be deemed sufficient; if the model is substantially misspecified, the resulting effects will lose any meaningful interpretation.
Furthermore, the baseline model needs to be specified.
For a reference group baseline, the reference group may either be included in the multi-group model, or a separate model can be used.
For a globally fitted baseline, a 'single-group' (i.e., fully restricted) model can be estimated.
Since such a model depends on the mixture of groups and their relative proportions, so will the implied expected response function.
Naturally, the model estimation procedure itself may also impact resulting effect values.
All models need to be specified using the same anchor item.
Step 5a) Calculate Suitable SDs for Standardization.

For standardized effects of non-invariance, similar to Cohen's d, an estimate s for the standard deviation of observed responses X needs to be computed; s i for the item-level effects and s T for sum-score-level effects.
A straightforward choice is the standard deviation of the entire sample; this ensures that the resulting effects are all on the same scale and thus directly comparable.
Depending on the specific setting, other choices may be more suitable.
Step 6) Calculate Effects of Non-Invariance.
Based on Step 5, multiple effects of non-invariance can be calculated.
In general, SEAD -i.e., EADpgq{s -can be used as the default measure of non-invariance: Reporting the table of all group's SEAD effects yields a fine-grained evaluation of MNI in the strict sense.
For a summary effect of non-invariance, accounting for differences in this group partition, the effect STEAD can be reported for the average non-invariance, along with the range of SEAD -cf.
Equation (21b) -denoting the extreme cases of non-invariance.

Note that for methodological research that requires numerical simplicity, the measures SRESD & SRTESD constitute beneficial approximations for SEAD & STEAD that can be used and interpreted analogously.

Step 6a) Calculate Impacts of Non-Invariance on Observed Means.
In specific cases where the impact of non-invariance on observed means is of interest, the values of the measure SED -i.e., EDpgq{s -can be reported in a table.
If desired, a summary effect STED 3 and the range of SED can be reported as well.
Furthermore, the impact of non-invariance on observed effects, such as Cohen's d, can be calculated -cf.
Equation (17).
Step 7) Interpret Results.
The calculated effects provide a nuanced evaluation of non-invariance by quantifying its severity.
Arguably, interpretation of measures is the most straightforward when effects are compared between groups, not evaluated as single values in isolation.
If a categorical verdict based on the calculated effects is desired, thresholds can be employed, cf.
Nye et al. (2019) for instance, differentiating between small, medium and large effects, although one-size-fits-all definitions of these categories should always be taken with a grain of salt.
It should be clearly stated that all such evaluations of non-invariance are relative to the chosen baseline; this fact should be reflected in any interpretation.
Researchers should also be aware that many measurement models assume normally distributed latent traits.
Ignoring non-normality in the calculation may substantially skew the resulting effects of non-invariance.
For valid results in such cases, approaches such as skew factor analysis (Hashemi et al., 2020) may be employed.
All things considered, the overarching goal is almost always to answer the question 'Is the impact of non-invariance practically relevant in this case?'.
This renders a final, binary verdict ultimately unavoidable, purely by the nature of decision-making.

However, in contrast to the usual statistical test results which by themselves effectively determine interpretation, reporting effects of non-invariance paints a much richer and more informative picture that -a priori -makes no claim as to what constitutes a meaningful violation.
Any dichotomy arises only in the subsequent, qualitative discussion of statistical results and is arguably much more transparent.

For instance, while it may be possible to deem a non-invariance effect of around .2 to be negligible given large mean difference effects bigger than .8, this decision could be critically challenged based on the reported statistical values alone.
Similarly, significant non-invariances may also be deemed acceptable in the discussion if the effect cancels out across items.
In that sense, effect sizes provide a more nuanced view of measurement invariance that goes beyond the usual all-or-nothing view of statistical testing.
Of course, what constitutes an acceptable range of non-invariance effect sizes is ambiguous and should always be questioned critically by both authors and readers.

In the following we discuss the results for the positivity dimension.
Overall, the practical impact of MNI at the item-level ranged from small to moderate.
The standardized sample-based effect sizes SEAD i puk | gerq ranged from 0.095 for hop3 to 0.622 for gra4_R, the reverse coded version of gra4.

The largest effects were observed for gra4_R (0.622), cap4_R (0.526), and for4_R (0.488), indicating that the expected response difference between the British and German responses amounted to roughly one half of a pooled item-level standard deviation for these items.
In contrast, hop3 showed only a very small effect (0.095), whereas zes3 showed a modest effect (0.210).
The direction indices provided additional information about the form of the non-invariance effects.
For for4_R, the sample-based direction index was exactly 1.000, indicating that the item consistently favored the British focal group across the relevant latent range.
A nearly uniform positive effect was also observed for cap4_R ( ÝÝÑ MNI cap4_R puk | gerq " 0.987).

The effect for hop3 was also negative, but weaker and less consistent ( ÝÝÑ MNI hop3 puk | gerq " ´0.589), reflecting substantial cancellation of positive and negative differences.

Taken together, this IRT-based illustration shows that effect-based assessments of intergroup comparability can also be implemented within a graded response modeling framework.
Even in this restricted unidimensional setting, the proposed measures provide detailed information about both the magnitude and the direction of MNI at the item-and scale-levels.

At the same time, it needs to be kept in mind that the results are conditional on the selected anchor item and on the omission of the acquiescence factor, which was necessary here because the currently available implementation of SIDS and UIDS is limited to unidimensional models.
In real-world applications beyond this methodological illustration, it might be advisable to perform sensitivity analyses using different anchor items.
In this paper, we introduced a model-agnostic taxonomic framework of effect size measures for MNI and DIF, capturing and extending more than 40 years of research on such effects.
Starting from the formal notion of 1 st -order MI, we introduced expected response functions, which are used to operationalize evaluations of 1 st -order non-invariance.

Based on this, we defined four basal measures quantifying such amounts of non-invariancewith respect to the selected baseline -directly in the metric of the indicators: ED & EAD for the amount of 1 st -order MNI within a group, and TED & TEAD for the total amount of 1 st -order MNI across a partition of groups, both with corresponding effect directions.

text.text: From the definition of ED and TED, we derived explicit formulas for the amount of MNI-induced bias in commonly used (standardized) mean difference effects, with respect to the chosen baseline expected response function.
Classifying the 37 effect size measures identified in the literature within this framework showed that all of them conceptually reduce to these four basal measures, 34 of them to just ED and EAD.
This pronounced conceptual overlap -i.e., "Jangle" (Kelley, 1927) -stands alongside vast taxonomic gaps in the literature, which the 112 conceptually distinct measures of our framework fill.

text.text: Our dual illustration on the same data demonstrated that the framework can be applied irrespective of the type of measurement model used, highlighting that the resulting effect size values depend on the choices made.
This emphasizes that choices about the baseline and the quantity of interest shape the conclusions, and that effect-based assessments make these choices explicit.
The taxonomy and the accompanying step-by-step guide are meant to support researchers in making such choices deliberately.
In our illustration, we discussed and illustrated how different scenarios and research goals call for different effect size measures.

Specifically, researchers need to decide a) whether the amount of MNI or its practical impact should be quantified, b) whether it makes sense to assume a reference category, c) whether to calculate effects using signed or unsigned differences, d) whether the effect should be standardized, e) whether a (normal) distribution of the latent variable is assumed (inferential vs. descriptive), f) whether itemor scale-level responses are to be investigated, and g) whether to focus on evaluating MNI within each group separately or in total across a partition of groups.

Some of these decisions can be informed directly by the research question or study design, e.g., assuming a reference category may make sense if a scale was developed in one context and is now transferred, for instance translated, to a new context.
Others remain relatively arbitrary.

Nonetheless, researchers should critically consider which choices can be justified and select an appropriate effect size measure accordingly, instead of relying solely on "standard" measures such as d MACS that may not suit their research goals.
The measures in our proposed taxonomy inherit most limitations of the effect sizes for MNI/DIF that it contains.
Most notably, the accuracy is inherently tied to the fit of the respective expected response functions.
When working with model-implied expected responses of models with insufficient model fit, estimates for MNI should be interpreted with caution.
This, of course, is a problem with latent variable modeling in general.
For inferential estimates, robustness could be increased by formulating confidence intervals.
Note that bootstrap-based confidence intervals exist for d MACS (M. Lai, 2024), which could be similarly implemented for ED and EAD in general.
There is also the general problem of effect sizes possibly overestimating null effects, as a result of sampling variability.
Different regularization methods exist (e.g., based on spike and slab priors) to counteract this (Van den Bergh et al., 2021), which can be applied for MNI effects as well.
Perhaps the most notable limitation is the ambiguity with respect to what constitutes a 'large' MNI effect.
There are simulation studies for d MACS , aiming to establish benchmarks (Nye et al., 2019), which should be taken with a grain of salt.

Instead of using simulation studies or empirical benchmarks to determine threshold values for what constitutes small, medium, or large effects, researchers need to define tolerable amounts of non-invariance -comparable to approaches such as approximate MI (Van de Schoot et al., 2013) -for each application or research context themselves, although further methodological research on ED and EAD may provide guidelines and meaningful defaults that researchers can use as a starting point for their own research.
